source_text: Sit ergo nostri operis exordium quaestio illa consequens ac secunda, utrum potestate unius dei mundus regatur anne multorum. nemo, qui quidem sapiat rationemque secum putet, non unum esse intellegat, qui et condiderit omnia et eadem qua condidit uirtute moderetur. quid enim multis opus est ad mundi regimen sustinendum? nisi forte arbitrabimur, si plures sint, minus habere singulos neruorum atque uirium: quod quidem faciunt ii qui esse multos uolunt, quia necesse est inbecillos esse, siquidem singuli sine auxilio reliquorum tantae molis gubernaculum sustinere non possunt. deus autem, qui est aeterna mens, ex omni utique parte perfectae consummataeque uirtutis est: quod si uerum est, unus sit necesse est. potestas enim uel uirtus absoluta retinet suam propriam firmitatem. id autem solidum existimandum est, cui nihil decedere, id perfectum, cui nihil possit accedere. quis dubitet potentissimum esse regem qui totius orbis habeat imperium? neque inmerito. cum illius sint Quae ubique sunt omnia cum ad eum solum omnes undique copiae congerantur. at si plures partiantur orbem, minus certe opum, minus uiriuni singuli habebunt, cum intra praescriptam portionem se quisque contineat. eodem modo etiam dii, si plures sint, minus ualebunt, aliis tantundem in se habentibus. uirtutis autem perfecta natura in eo potest esse in quo totum est quam in eo in quo pars exigua de toto est. deus uero si perfectus est, ut esse debet, non potest esse nisi unus, ut in eo sint omnia. deorum igitur uirtutes ac potestates infirmiores sint necesse est, quia tantum singulis deerit, quantum in ceteris fuerit: ita quanto plures tanto minores erunt. quid quod summa illa rerum potestas ac diuina uis ne semel quidem diuidi potest? quidquid enim capit diuisionem, et interitum capiat necesse est. si autem interitus procul est a deo, quia incorruptibilis est et aeternus, consequens est ut diuidi potestas diuina non possit. deus ergo unus est, si nihil esse aliut potest quod : tantundem capiat potestatis: et ii tamen qui multos esse arbitrantur officia inter se dicunt esse partitos. de quibus omnibus suo loco disputabimus. illud interim quod ad praesentem locum pertinet teneo: si partiti sunt inter se officia, eodem reuoluitur res, ut ex iis quilibet sufficere omnibus nequeat. perfectus igitur non erit qui cessantibus ceteris non potest omnia gubernare. ita fit ut ad regendum mundum unius perfecta uirtute opus sit quam inbecillitate multorum. qui autem putat hanc tantam magnitudinem non posse ab uno regi, fallitur neque quanta sit uis ac potestas diuinae maiestatis intellegit, si existimat singularem deum qui facere mundum potuit, eundem regere non posse quem fecit. at si concipiat animo quanta sit diuini huius operis inmensitas (eamque) cum antea nihil esset, tamen uirtute atque consilio dei ex nihilo esse conflatam, quod opus nisi ab uno inchoari perficique non potuit, iam intelleget multo facilius esse ab uno regi quod est ab uno constitutum. dicat fortasse aliquis ne tabricari quidem tam inmensum opus mundi nisi a pluribus potuisse. quamlibet multos, quamlibet magnos faciat, quidquid in multis magnitudinis potestatis uirtutis maiestatisque posuerit, id totum in unum confero et in uno esse dico, ut tantum in eo sit istarum rerum, quantum nec cogitari nec dici potest. qua in re quoniam et sensu deficimur et uerbis, quia neque tantam intellegentiae lucem pectus humanum neque explanationem tantarum rerum capit lingua mortalis, id ipsum intellegere nos oportet ac dicere. uideo rursus quid e contrario dici possit, tales esse illos plures qualem nos uolumus unum. at hoc fieri nullo pacto potest, quod singulorum potestas progredi longius non ualebit occurrentibus sibi potestatibus ceterorum. necesse est enim ut suos quisque limites aut transgredi nequeat aut si transgressus fuerit, suis alterum finibus pellat. non uident qui deos multos esse credunt fieri posse ut aliquid diuersum uelint, ex qua re disceptatio inter eos et certamen oriatur; sicut Homerus bellantes inter se deos finxit, cum alii Troiam capi uellent, alii repugnarent. unius igitur arbitrio mundum regi necesse est. nisi enim singularum partium potestas ad unam prouidentiam referatur, non poterit summa ipsa constare, uno quoque nihil curante amplius quam quod ad eum proprie pertinet, sicut ne res quidem militaris nisi unum habeat ducem atque rectorem. quodsi in uno exercitu tot fuerint imperatores quot legiones, quot cohortes, quot cunei, quot alae, primum nec instrui poterit acies uno quoque periculum recusante nec regi facile aut temperari, quod suis propriis consiliis utantur omnes, quorum diuersitate plus noceant quam prosint: sic in hoc rerum naturae imperio nisi unus fuerit ad quem totius summae cura referatur, uniuersa soluentur et conruent. dicere autem multorum arbitrio regi mundum tale est, quale si quis adfirmet in uno corpore multas esse mentes, quoniam multa et uaria sint ministeria membrorum, ut singulos corporis sensus singulae mentes regere credantur, item multi adfectus, quibus commoueri solemus uel ad iram uel ad cupiditatem uel ad laetitiam uel ad metum uel ad miserationem, ut in his omnibus totidem mentes putentur operari. quod si quis profecto dicat, ne ipsam quidem quae una est habere uideatur. quodsi in uno corpore tantarum rerum gubernationem mens una possidet et uniuersis simul intenta est, cur aliquis existimet mundum non posse ab uno regi, a pluribus posse? quod quia intellegunt isti adsertores deorum, ita eos praeesse singulis rebus ac partibus dicunt, ut tamen unus sit rector eximius. iam ergo ceteri non dii erunt, sed satellites ac ministri, quos ille unus maximus ac potens omnium iis officiis praefecerit, ut ipsi eius imperio ac nutibus seruiant. si uniuersi pares non sunt, non igitur dii omnes sunt: nec enim potest hoc idem esse quod seruit et quod dominatur. nam si deus nomen est summae potestatis, incorruptibilis esse debet, perfectus inpassibilis nulli rei subiectus. ergo dii non sunt quos parere um maximo deo necessitas cogit. sed quia non frustra falluntur qui hoc ita putant, causam huius erroris paulo post aperiemus. nunc unitatem diuinae potestatis testimoniis conprobemus.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, let the beginning of our work be that question which follows and is second, whether the world is governed by the power of one God or of many. No one, who indeed is wise and thinks reason with himself, does not understand that there is one who both founded all things and moderates the same with the virtue with which he founded them. For what need is there for many for sustaining the governance of the world? Unless perhaps we might think that if there are more, individual ones have less nerve and strength: which indeed those who want there to be many do, because it is necessary for them to be weak, since individual ones cannot sustain the helm of such a great mass without the help of the remaining ones. But God, who is eternal mind, is from every part perfect and consummated virtue: which if it is true, it is necessary for there to be one. For absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness. And that which is solid is to be thought, to which nothing can be lacking, that which is perfect, to which nothing can be added. Who doubts that the most powerful king is he who has the command of the whole world? And not without cause. Since all things that are everywhere are his, and all resources from everywhere are gathered to him alone. But if more share the world, individual ones will certainly have less wealth, less strength, since each one is contained within his prescribed portion. In the same way also, if there are more gods, they will be less strong, having as much in themselves as others have. The perfect nature of virtue can be in that in which the whole is, rather than in that in which a small part of the whole is. But God, if he is perfect, as he ought to be, cannot be except one, so that all things may be in him. Therefore, the virtues and powers of the gods are necessarily weaker, because as much is lacking to individual ones as is in the others: so the more there are, the smaller they will be. What of the fact that the highest power of things and divine strength cannot even once be divided? For whatever undergoes division also undergoes destruction. But if destruction is far from God, because he is incorruptible and eternal, it follows that divine power cannot be divided. Therefore, God is one, if nothing else can have as much power: and those who think there are many say that offices are divided among them. About all these things we will dispute in their own place. This meanwhile I hold, which pertains to the present place: if offices are divided among them, the matter returns to the same, so that each one cannot suffice for all. Therefore, he will not be perfect who, with the others failing, cannot govern all things. So it happens that for governing the world, the perfect virtue of one is needed, rather than the weakness of many. But he who thinks that this so great magnitude cannot be governed by one is deceived, and does not understand how great the strength and power of divine majesty is, if he thinks that a single God who could make the world cannot govern what he made. But if he conceives in his mind how great the immensity of this divine work is (and that) with nothing previously existing, nevertheless it was made from nothing by the virtue and counsel of God, which work could not be begun or completed except by one, now he will understand more easily that it is easier for one to govern what was established by one. Perhaps someone will say that not even a work as immense as the world could be made by fewer than many. However many, however great he makes them, whatever of magnitude, power, virtue, and majesty he puts in many, I confer all that upon one and say that it exists in one, so that there is as much of those things in him as cannot be thought or said. In this matter, since we fail in both sense and words, because the human breast does not grasp so great a light of understanding, nor does the mortal tongue grasp the explanation of such great things, we ought to understand and say this. I see again what can be said on the contrary, that those many are such as we want one to be. But this cannot happen in any way, because the power of individual ones will not be able to proceed further, with the powers of the others occurring to them. For it is necessary that each one have his own limits, which he cannot transgress, or if he has transgressed, he drives another back with his own limits. Those who believe there are many gods do not see that it is possible for them to will something different, from which a dispute and contest arise among them; just as Homer fashioned the gods fighting among themselves, when some wanted Troy to be taken, others resisted. Therefore, it is necessary for the world to be governed by the judgment of one. For unless the power of individual parts is referred to one providence, the sum itself will not be able to consist, with each one caring for nothing more than what pertains to him, just as not even a military thing can have more than one leader and ruler. And if in one army there are as many commanders as there are legions, cohorts, wedges, or wings, first the battle line will not be able to be drawn up, with each one refusing danger, nor will it be easy to rule or temper, because all use their own counsel, the diversity of which harms more than it helps: so in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole sum is referred, all things will be dissolved and will fall. But to say that the world is governed by the judgment of many is such as if someone were to affirm that in one body there are many minds, since there are many and varied ministries of the members, so that individual minds are believed to rule individual senses of the body, and also many affections, by which we are moved either to anger or to desire or to joy or to fear or to pity, so that in all these things as many minds as there are are thought to operate. Which if someone were to say, he would not even seem to have one mind. But if in one body one mind possesses the governance of so many things and is intent on all things at the same time, why does someone think that the world cannot be governed by one, but can be by many? Because those who assert the gods understand this, they say that they preside over individual things and parts, so that nevertheless there is one excellent ruler. Now therefore the others will not be gods, but satellites and ministers, whom that one greatest and most powerful of all has placed over those offices, so that they serve his command and nods. If all are not equal, they are not therefore all gods: nor can this same thing be which serves and which dominates. For if God is a name of highest power, it ought to be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to no thing. Therefore, those are not gods whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God. But because those who think this are not deceived in vain, we will reveal the cause of this error a little later. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.

choices.why: to maintain the unity of divine power
to explain the diversity of the world

pass_b_english: Let the second and following question be the starting point of our work: whether the world is governed by the power of one God or of many. No one who is truly wise and exercises reason can fail to recognize that there is a single Being who both founded all things and governs them with the very power by which he created them. What need would there be for many to sustain the governance of the world? Unless one supposes that if there were several, each would possess less strength and vigor—a concession that proponents of many gods are forced to make, since individually they could not bear the helm of so vast a mass without the help of the others. God, however, is eternal mind, and from every angle he is perfect, consummate virtue. If that is true, he must be one. Absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness; what is solid lacks nothing, and what is perfect admits no addition. Who doubts that the mightiest king is he who holds command over the whole world? And not without reason: all things everywhere belong to him, and all resources from every quarter are gathered to him alone. If more than one were to divide the world, each would certainly possess less wealth and less strength, confined as each is to an allotted portion. The same holds for gods: if they were many, each would be weaker, having no more in himself than the others possess. The perfect nature of virtue can reside only in that which contains the whole, not in that which holds but a small part of the whole. Since God is perfect, as he must be, he cannot be anything but one, so that all things may be in him. Consequently, the virtues and powers of many gods would necessarily be inferior, for each would lack exactly as much as the others contain; the more there are, the smaller each becomes. Moreover, the supreme power of the universe and divine strength cannot be divided even once. Whatever undergoes division necessarily undergoes destruction. But destruction is utterly foreign to God, because he is incorruptible and eternal; therefore divine power cannot be divided. God is one, then, if nothing else can possess equal power. Those who argue for many gods claim that offices are divided among them, a matter we will dispute in its proper place. For now I hold this point, which bears on the present argument: if offices are divided, the case reduces to the same problem—no single one can suffice for all. A being who cannot govern all things when the others fail is not perfect. Thus the world requires the perfect virtue of one, not the weakness of many. Anyone who thinks this immense magnitude cannot be ruled by one is deceived and fails to grasp the strength and power of divine majesty. If a single God could make the world, he can certainly govern what he made. Once one conceives in his mind the immensity of this divine work—how, though nothing existed before, it was formed from nothing by God's virtue and counsel, a work that could be begun and completed by one alone—he will understand all the more easily that what was established by one is far more easily governed by one. Someone may object that even the making of so immense a world could not have been accomplished by fewer than many. However many or great he imagines them, whatever magnitude, power, virtue, and majesty he distributes among them, I gather all of it into one and declare that it exists in one, so that there is in him as much of those qualities as can be neither thought nor expressed. In this matter we fail both in perception and in language, for the human breast cannot grasp so great a light of understanding, nor can mortal tongue compass the explanation of such things; yet we must understand and speak this truth. I see again what might be urged on the contrary: that those many are each such as we would have the one be. But this is impossible, because the power of each cannot advance further when confronted by the powers of the others. Each must have his own limits, which he cannot transgress; if he does transgress, he simply drives another back within his own bounds. Those who believe in many gods do not see that it becomes possible for them to will different things, giving rise to dispute and conflict among them—just as Homer invented gods warring with one another, some wanting Troy taken, others resisting. The world must therefore be governed by the judgment of one. Unless the power of the individual parts is referred to a single providence, the whole cannot hold together, each part caring for nothing beyond what properly belongs to it, just as no army can function with more than one leader and ruler. If in one army there were as many commanders as there are legions, cohorts, wedges, or wings, the battle line could not even be drawn up, each commander shirking danger, and it would be impossible to direct or control them, since all would follow their own counsels, whose diversity would harm more than help. So in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole is referred, all things will dissolve and collapse. To say that the world is governed by the judgment of many is like asserting that one body contains many minds because its members perform many and varied functions—as if separate minds were thought to rule the separate senses of the body, and as many minds as there are emotions—anger, desire, joy, fear, pity—were thought to operate within us. If someone actually said that, he would not even seem to possess one mind himself. But if one mind in a single body governs so many things and attends to all simultaneously, why should anyone think the world cannot be governed by one but can be by many? Because the advocates of many gods recognize this, they say the gods preside over individual things and parts, yet insist there is still one supreme ruler. Then the others are not gods at all, but satellites and ministers whom that one greatest and most powerful has placed over those offices to serve his command and bidding. If all are not equal, they are not all gods; the same thing cannot be both servant and master. For if God is the name of highest power, he must be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to nothing. Therefore those whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God are not gods. Yet because those who think this way are not deceived in vain, we will reveal the cause of their error shortly. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text of Lactantius, Divine Institutes 1.3. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent, high-quality rendering that preserves all nuances of the original Latin, including the philosophical distinctions regarding perfection, division, and the analogy of the body and the army. All arguments, including the Homeric reference and the military analogy, are fully captured.
